catalog_quote: 4. The stress group. The stress group is posited as a sub-rank between syllable and word level. Both primary and secondary stress groups consist of a nuclear stressed syllable preceeded by up to three pre-stressed syllables. 4.1 Primary stress group. Functions as nucleus of the word ... 4.2 Secondary stress group. Functions in the pre-nucleus of the word ... 4.3 Partial correspondence of phonological stress group and grammatical morpheme. It can be stated that each stress group corresponds to a free morpheme, although it is not true that every free morpheme forms a separate stress group. In general a word consisting of three free morphemes (say) will have three stressed syllables, the final stressed syllable taking primary stress and preceeding ones taking secondary stress. e.g. "dentist" čhi4ne4.ški3.ni4?ño4 [braces: 2ary str. under ne4.ški3 / 1ary str. under ni4?ño4] ... Bound morphemes never take secondary stress, but attach as pre-stressed syllables to the following stress group 5. The word. The phonological word consists of a primary stress group as nucleus, optionally preceeded by up to two secondary stress groups, and optionally followed by a single post-stressed syllable. e.g. "he explained it to you(pl)" ko3ve1no4hmi1-no2 [braces under ko3ve1 and no4hmi1, line from -no2; hand-drawn connectors join ko3ve1 to 'primary stress group', no4hmi1 to 'secondary stress group', -no2 to 'post-stressed syllable']
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: San Jerónimo Tecóatl Mazatec is not in the catalog. All three works with stress in the title are the same work — Alderete's 1999 UMass dissertation 'Morphologically governed accent in Optimality Theory' (ROA-309) and its 2001 Routledge book version. I downloaded the full dissertation (5 ROA PDFs, 282 pp., and a full-text search for stress/accent the whole text: it never mentions Mazatec, Tecóatl, Oaxaca or Otomanguean (its case studies are Cupeño, Russian, Tokyo Japanese, Aguaruna, Limburg Dutch, Tahltan). Glottolog's own records (656934/656935/316463) label the language link 'computerized assignment from \"governed\"', i.e. a keyword-matching artefact. Relevance of all three items: other language; priority none. The only first-hand stress statement for this language is Bull 1978 (SIL archive 54686, already held by the project from the earlier reading, scanned page scan re-checked by eye): stress is organised in morpheme-based stress groups, each root carrying a stressed syllable after up to three unstressed prefixal syllables, with primary stress on the final stress group of the word and secondary on preceding ones, plus an optional single post-stressed enclitic syllable (sections 4-5, pp. 19-20). new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is group-final: a stress group is one stressed syllable preceded by up to three unstressed (pre-stressed) syllables, and roughly corresponds to a free morpheme (root). Primary word stress falls on the stressed syllable of the last stress group, i.e. on the final syllable of the word, except that a single reduced 'post-stressed' syllable (person enclitic/suffix such as 2pl -no2, 1pl.excl -hę4) may follow it, in which case primary stress is on the penult. Prefixes and other bound morphemes are unstressed. The language is tonal (four level tones plus two lexical glides, contrastive per syllable; nasal/oral, ballistic/controlled and interruption contrasts occur only in primary-stressed syllables).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Each preceding free morpheme (root) in a compound/complex word forms a secondary stress group whose final syllable bears secondary stress; up to two secondary stress groups per word (e.g. chi4ne4.š?i3.ni4?ño4 'dentist' = 2ary + 1ary). A pre-final morpheme may instead be absorbed into the primary stress group as a pre-stressed syllable (khoa4.hčą1 ~ kho4hčą1 'war'); secondary-stressed syllables lose nasal/oral, interruption and ballistic/controlled contrasts.
new_statements.exceptions: Optional single post-stressed syllable after the primary-stressed syllable (person markers, e.g. -no2 'you pl.', 1pl.excl -hę4 'appears to be phonologically independent although it behaves grammatically as a verb suffix'); free morphemes sometimes absorbed into the following stress group ('More study is needed to determine under what circumstances'); author flags the whole analysis as tentative ('not meant to be a scientific write-up').
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word built from stress groups (≈ root + prefixes); statement is for word-level phonology in isolation forms, phrase-level tone/stress explicitly excluded ('Other tone glides occur at phonological phrase and sentence level, and are not dealt with in this paper'). Consistent with final stress reported for Huautla Mazatec (Pike & Pike 1947). The 2019 Gramática popular (same variety) presupposes an 'acento prosódico' on verbs/roots that proclitic auxiliaries and dependent pronouns lack, but states no placement rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Bull 1978 describes the Mazatec of San Jerónimo Tecóatl town (district of Teotitlán), i.e. the reference variety of Glottolog sanj1286 / ISO maa (Ethnologue now labels maa 'Eloxochitlán Mazatec'; SIL Mexico page title 'Mazatec of Eloxochitlán de Flores Magón'). The 2019 Gramática popular is the same San Jerónimo Tecóatl variety. Martínez Carrera 2020 (listed by Glottolog under sanj1286) is a different variety (San Juan La Unión, Zoquiapam = INALI 'mazateco del oeste/de Zoquiapam') and was not used for the statement.

tone_statements.quote: Las lenguas mazatecas son tonales. Hay cuatro tonos básicos en el mazateco de Eloxochitlán: alto, medio-alto, medio y bajo. El tono alto se escribe con un acento agudo sobre la vocal, como en yá [ja˥] ‘árbol’. El tono medio-alto se escribe con un acento grave sobre la vocal, como en jàn [hã˦] ‘tres’. El tono bajo se escribe con una raya debajo de la vocal, como en ꞌje̱ [hʔe˩] ‘jilote’. El tono medio es representado sin tilde alguna, como en je [he˧] ‘grande’. Las vocales se escriben dobles para indicar un deslizamiento de tono, como en chjo̲ón [t͡ʃhõ˩˥] ‘mujer’ donde el tono inicial es bajo y se desliza hasta el tono alto. La vocal, en realidad, no tiene duración adicional.
tone_statements.translation: The Mazatec languages are tonal. There are four basic tones in Eloxochitlán Mazatec: high, mid-high, mid and low. High tone is written with an acute accent over the vowel, as in yá [ja˥] 'tree'. Mid-high tone is written with a grave accent over the vowel, as in jàn [hã˦] 'three'. Low tone is written with a line under the vowel, as in ꞌje̱ [hʔe˩] 'young corn ear'. Mid tone is represented with no diacritic, as in je [he˧] 'big'. Vowels are written double to indicate a tone glide, as in chjo̱ón [t͡ʃhõ˩˥] 'woman', where the initial tone is low and glides up to high. The vowel does not actually have additional duration.
tone_statements.locator: Section 3 'Tonos', pp. 4-5; Apéndice A p. 7; Apéndice B 'Tonos' p. 8
tone_statements.summary: Four level tones (high, mid-high, mid, low) plus contour glides (e.g. low-high, mid-high rising) on single syllables without added vowel length.

High tone is written with an acute accent over the vowel, as in yá [ja˥] 'tree'. Mid-high tone is written with a grave accent over the vowel, as in jàn [hã˦] 'three'. Low tone is written with a line under the vowel, as in ꞌje̱ [hʔe˩] 'young corn ear'. Mid tone is represented with no diacritic, as in je [he˧] 'big'. tone.summary: Four level tones (high, mid-high, mid, low) plus contour glides (e.g. low-high, mid-high rising) on single syllables without added vowel length.
tone.says: States that Eloxochitlán Mazatec has four basic level tones — high (acute), mid-high (grave), mid (unmarked), low (underline) — plus tone glides written with doubled vowels that carry no extra length (e.g. chjo̱ón [t͡ʃhõ˩˥] 'woman', low rising to high); in vowel clusters tone is written on the final vowel. Orthographic statement with IPA tone letters, no sandhi or stress analysis.
